newsitem.title: FRANCE: France, Italy set out European defence initiative.
newsitem.headline: France, Italy set out European defence initiative.

text.p: France and Italy, on the eve of the 40th anniversary of the European Union's founding Treaty of Rome, set out on Monday a joint initiative by six EU members to build a common European defence in stages.

Outlined by Foreign Ministers Herve de Charette and Lamberto Dini in an article in the newspaper Le Monde, it would mean that all 15 EU states eventually subscribed to the mutual security guarantee contained in the founding treaty of the Western European Union (WEU) defence grouping.
The ministers said they intended to use an anniversary meeting in Rome on Tuesday to give "a decisive impulse to the negotiation under way".

The session should agree on plans to make a common foreign policy more effective by establishing a policy planning unit, incorporating peacekeeping missions into the treaty and creating a post of high representative for EU foreign policy, they said.

But the main thrust of their proposal was to incorporate the 10-nation WEU, founded in 1948 one year before the U.S.-led NATO alliance, gradually into the European Union "to make defence no longer a theory but a real prospect".

Britain has threatened to veto incorporating the WEU into the EU, arguing that the two bodies do not have the same membership and that the European Union is not the appropriate forum for handling defence.
Neutral states Finland, Sweden and Austria, which joined the EU only recently and are not NATO members, also oppose being forced into a defence pact.
De Charette and Dini said the answer lay in achieving the change in stages, with the WEU and the EU sharing certain common institutions during a transitional period.
"The arrival point would be transferring into the (EU) treaty the mutual guarantee commitment according to article 5 of the WEU treaty," they said.

"In this spirit, a group of countries -- France, Germany, Belgium, Luxembourg, Spain, Italy -- suggest a route involving several stages and a method: giving the Council of heads of state and government the decision to move to each new stage," the article said.

The ministers said this month's crisis in Albania had been another test case for EU foreign policy and highlighted "the need for the European Union to have more effective analysis and forecasting instruments".
They said the EU should define "common strategies" on areas of fundamental joint interest.
